For a project explicitly scoped as requirements and analysis-only, standard requirements engineering defines the **requirements baseline** as the foundational input from which more technical, physical system design specifications will later be built [1]. The absolute boundary of an analysis-only scope is defined by a simple rule: **do not write a single line of backend transformation or database logic until stakeholders have formally signed off on the validated requirements** [2]. 

To count as credible and industry-aligned at this preliminary stage, deliverables must remain strictly logical and outcome-oriented, describing *what* the system must do and *why*, rather than *how* it will be physically engineered [3, 4]. 

---

### 1. Data Strategy & Strategic Alignment
A requirements-only data strategy focuses exclusively on answering: **"Why are we investing in this initiative?"** [5, 6]. It is designed to align high-level business priorities and company OKRs with required data capabilities [5, 6].
*   **The Minimum Viable (MV) Artifact:** A conceptual **Modernization Plan / Roadmap** [5, 7] and a high-level **AI and Analytics Strategy** [5, 7]. This document maps key business initiatives to the data capabilities required to solve them [5, 8].
*   **What is Omitted (Non-Production Version):** It excludes detailed financial ledger statements, finalized vendor quotes, detailed hardware procurement costs, and granular software licensing agreements [9, 10].

### 2. Data Governance & Policy Definition
At this stage, governance focuses on answering: **"What rules should guide our data and system usage?"** [5, 6]. It outlines standards, ownership boundaries, and operational accountability [5].
*   **The Minimum Viable (MV) Artifact:** A logical **Governance Framework**, an **Ownership & Stewardship Model**, and a core **Business Glossary** [5, 11]. It identifies key roles (such as designating specific business units as data owners or stewards) [5, 12] and documents standard compliance requirements—such as data privacy policies or medical PII/HIPAA constraints—that the future system must obey [12-14].
*   **What is Omitted (Non-Production Version):** It excludes physical user-access directories (e.g., Active Directory LDAP configurations) [15, 16], active role-based access control (RBAC) code policies [16, 17], and automated metadata/lineage crawlers [18-20].

### 3. Business / Product Requirements Specification (BRD or PRD)
The BRD or PRD provides downstream engineering and design teams with complete clarity on the project's scope, business drivers, constraints, and success criteria [3, 21].
*   **The Minimum Viable (MV) Artifact:** A structured document capturing the **Problem Statement**, **User Personas/Insights**, isolated **Functional Requirements** prioritized on a standard scale of 1 to 5 (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Future) [21-23], **Non-Functional Requirements** (such as volume skew, compliance rules, and latencies) [21, 24], and **testable success metrics** (omitting ambiguous goals like "easy to use") [25]. 
*   **What is Omitted (Non-Production Version):** It should never be structured as a delivery backlog (which lists developer tasks) or a physical feature spec sheet (which describes technical outputs rather than business outcomes) [4]. It lacks finalized physical database schemas, exact API endpoints, and system-level interface code [3, 24, 26].

### 4. Use Case Validation
In requirements engineering, a use case is not considered "validated" if it is based solely on static text and unverified stakeholder wishes [27]. However, since you cannot build production code yet, you must validate using lightweight logical assets [2, 27].
*   **The Minimum Viable (MV) Artifact:** A package containing **Visual Prototypes (or workflows/diagrams)** [25] paired with **Representative Sample Data** (such as a mock CSV file or a sample dashboard view demonstrating expected business logic) [27]. Validation is achieved by letting end-users analyze this sample to confirm it meets their expected usage patterns [27], resolving stakeholder conflicts [25], and recording a **formal requirements sign-off** in JIRA or a similar tracker [2, 27].
*   **What is Omitted (Non-Production Version):** It completely bypasses physical ETL development, active transformation scripts, database staging, and live user interface code [2, 27].

### 5. Gap Analysis & Target Architecture Alignment
This analysis bridges the gap between current state limitations and the target business objectives, identifying logical system boundaries [5].
*   **The Minimum Viable (MV) Artifact:** A logical-only **Data Architecture Blueprint** [5, 11] outlining integration/information flows [5] alongside a **Technology Stack Definition** [5, 11]. It contains a dimensional matrix comparing "As-Is" legacy challenges (e.g., manual data extraction, disconnected silos) against "To-Be" target design paradigms (e.g., a centralized warehouse versus a distributed data mesh) [28-30].
*   **What is Omitted (Non-Production Version):** It excludes virtual machine backups [31], system software versioning specs [32], physical server hardware layouts, network switch configurations, cabling designs, and power consumption calculations [31, 33].

Performance:  Record Service is designed to be on the main data access path, meaning it needs to process every byte of data. Record Service scales horizontally to be able to run on the largest Hadoop clusters and high efficiency. It uses the Apache Impala IO layer, which utilizes low-level optimizations such as HDFS short-circuit reads and dynamic code generation to improve thread throughput and reduce CPU utilization. Record Service brings these performance benefits to the other components in Hadoop and accelerates their performance, despite adding a new layer in the stack. Simplicity: Record Service provides a higher level, logical abstraction for data. 2.2. Help end-users define the requirements Assume the end-users don't know everything they want or even that they will clearly define it to you. You can't get 100% of the requirements right the first time. Talk with the end-user about their objectives and their difficulties. Understanding the current status of end-user operations will provide valuable insights. The end-user might say “We want X data”. Help the end-user define requirements by asking the following questions: Business impact : How does having this data impact the business? What is the measurable improvement in the bottom line, business OKR, etc? Knowing the business impact helps in determining if this project is worth doing. Semantic understanding : What does the data represent? What business process generates this data? Knowing this will help you model the data and understand its relation to other tables in your warehouse. Data source : Where does the data originate? (an application DB, external vendor via SFTP/Cloud store dumps, API data pull, manual upload, etc). Frequency of data pipeline : How fresh does the data need to be? (n minutes, hourly, daily, weekly, etc). Is there a business case for not allowing a higher frequency? What is the highest frequency of data load acceptable by end-users? Historical data : Does historical data need to be stored? When loading data into a warehouse, the answer is usually yes. Data caveats : Does the data have any caveats? (e.g. seasonality affecting size, data skew, inability to join, or data unavailability). Are there any known issues with upstream data sources, such as late arriving data, or missing data? Access pattern : How will the end user access the data? Is access via SQL, dashboard tool, APIs, or cloud storage? In the case of SQL or dashboard access, What are the commonly used filter columns (e.g. date, some business entity)? What is the expected access latency? Business rules check (QA) : What data quality metrics do the end-users care about? What are business logic-based data quality checks? Which numeric fields should be checked for divergence (e.g. can't differ by more than x%) across data pulls? Data output requirements : What is the data output schema? (column names, API field names, Cloud storage file name/size, etc)

Best Practices for Documenting Business Requirements As you work your way through the template, here are eight best-practices that will guide you in documenting the business requirements and set your development project up for success: Assign resources to write the business requirements who understand all stakeholder needs and the project's software development language. Meet with stakeholders from every business unit impacted by the project—preferably in one-on-one meetings to ensure everyone is heard. Reconcile conflicts among stakeholders who disagree on a requirement; it's critical to do so before development begins. Identify the target audience for each requirement, which will factor into the end-user testing process. Ensure each requirement is testable so that achieving it can be validated. Facilitate testing by defining each requirement separately; combining two or more into one definition may make validation impossible. Specify the exact success metrics for satisfying each requirement; “easy to use” is ambiguous and difficult to define as to when it's achieved. Leverage images, graphs, charts, diagrams, workflows, use-cases and visual prototypes to articulate the documented requirements to non-technical stakeholders.

Enterprise Data Management Architecture A data management architecture is your organization's blueprint for collecting, storing, securing, arranging, integrating, and using data through interconnected management systems. There's no one-size-fits-all architecture; it's shaped by business needs, goals, and constraints. Common approaches to enterprise data management architecture are: Monolithic architecture . All data is handled by a single centralized data store. It's simple in implementation but comes with high latency and limited scalability. Distributed data mesh . Domain-specific data owners handle their data products and pipelines, with the architecture consisting of smaller decentralized components. It offers better scalability and flexibility, but is more complex in implementation.

Monolithic Architecture vs Distributed Data Mesh Modern enterprise data management architectures increasingly rely on cloud-based data platforms to support scalability and advanced analytics. Cloud data management enables organizations to process large volumes of structured and unstructured data with scalable data storage, while optimizing infrastructure costs. At the same time, it introduces additional requirements for data security, access controls, and regulatory compliance, especially in multi-cloud or hybrid environments.
